course.description: Original A1.1 supplementary content aligned with the seven-unit learning outcomes of Schritte plus Neu A1.1, with Bangla translations and approximate Bangla pronunciation for added vocabulary.

lessons.title: Guten Tag! – Greetings & Introductions
objectives: Greet people at different times of day
Introduce yourself and ask for someone’s name
Say where you come from
Talk about languages you speak
Spell your name
Fill a simple registration form
Complete a simple personal-details form and ask for spelling or repetition.
Ask someone for a person on the phone and leave a simple message.
Read a business card and complete a registration form with personal details.
Spell names and ask someone to repeat or speak slowly.
Use the German alphabet and practise the vowel combinations ei, eu and au.

grammar.title: Personal pronouns & sein
grammar.explanation: ich bin, du bist, Sie sind

grammar.title: W-Questions
grammar.explanation: Wie, Woher, Was

grammar.title: Verb conjugation (present)
grammar.explanation: heißen, kommen, sprechen, sein

grammar.title: Spelling and personal details
grammar.explanation: Use the alphabet to spell names and complete simple forms with first name, surname, street, house number, city, country, phone number and email. Ask for repetition with Bitte noch einmal, langsam.

grammar.title: Countries, languages and aus
grammar.explanation: Use aus with a country to say where you come from. Language names are nouns and begin with a capital letter.
examples: Ich spreche Bengali und ein bisschen Deutsch.

grammar.title: Verb position in a statement
grammar.explanation: In a normal German statement, the conjugated verb is in position two. The first position can be a name or another detail; the verb stays second.

grammar.title: Formal Sie and informal du
grammar.explanation: Use du with friends, classmates and children when invited. Use Sie with adults you do not know or in a formal service situation. Formal Sie and its verb form begin with a capital letter.

grammar.title: Yes/no questions and W-questions
grammar.explanation: A yes/no question starts with the verb. A W-question puts the question word first and the conjugated verb second.

grammar.title: Possessive articles
grammar.explanation: mein/meine, dein/deine, Ihr/Ihre change according to gender

grammar.title: Personal pronouns (er/sie/wir/ihr/sie)
grammar.explanation: He / She / We / You (plural) / They

grammar.title: Present tense and wohnen in
grammar.explanation: Verb endings change with the subject: ich wohne, du wohnst, er/sie wohnt, wir wohnen, ihr wohnt, Sie wohnen. Use in with a city.

grammar.title: Asking about well-being
grammar.explanation: Wie geht es dir? is informal; Wie geht es Ihnen? is formal. Common replies include Danke, gut and Es geht mir nicht so gut.

grammar.title: Age with sein
grammar.explanation: German uses sein, not haben, to say how old someone is. Add Jahre alt after the number; Jahr is singular with one.
examples: Meine Tochter ist ein Jahr alt.

grammar.title: Possessives agree with the thing owned
grammar.explanation: mein/dein/Ihr take -e with many feminine nouns and plural nouns: meine Mutter, deine Geschwister, Ihre Kinder. Ihr is capitalized in formal writing.

grammar.title: Formal and informal well-being questions
grammar.explanation: Use dir with du and Ihnen with formal Sie. The response can start with Danke; the subject pronoun mir follows the phrase es geht.
examples: Wie geht es dir? – Danke, gut.
Wie geht es Ihnen? – Es geht mir nicht so gut.

grammar.title: Indefinite article & negation
grammar.explanation: ein/eine vs kein/keine
examples: Haben wir Zucker? – Nein, wir haben keinen Zucker.

grammar.title: Plural forms
grammar.explanation: Many food items have irregular plurals

grammar.title: Polite requests with möchten
grammar.explanation: möchten is conjugated: ich möchte, du möchtest, er/sie möchte, wir möchten, Sie möchten. Ask for quantities politely with Ich möchte ... or Ich hätte gern ...
examples: Ich hätte gern eine Flasche Wasser.

grammar.title: Quantities and prices
grammar.explanation: Use ein Kilo, ein Pfund, 100 Gramm, eine Flasche, eine Packung and ein Becher. Ask Was kostet ...? for one item and Was kosten ...? for plural.

grammar.title: Zero article with food in general
grammar.explanation: When you mean food in general or an uncounted amount, German often uses no article: Wir brauchen Reis. With a specific countable singular item, use ein/eine; with a negative item use kein/keine.

grammar.title: Question word order while shopping
grammar.explanation: A yes/no question starts with the conjugated verb. A W-question begins with the question word and keeps the verb in position two.

grammar.title: Polite requests with hätte gern
grammar.explanation: Ich hätte gern ... is a polite, common way to order or shop. Use bitte and a quantity to make the request complete.
examples: Ich hätte gern 200 Gramm Käse, bitte.

grammar.title: Plural nouns in food lists
grammar.explanation: Learn a food noun together with its plural. Some forms change the vowel, some add -e/-en, and some stay the same.

grammar.title: Definite articles
grammar.explanation: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter)

grammar.title: Predicative adjectives
grammar.explanation: Adjective after sein does not change

grammar.title: Place words and pronouns
grammar.explanation: hier means here and dort means there. Replace known nouns with er (masculine), es (neuter) or sie (feminine).
examples: Der Schrank ist hier. Er ist groß.
Die Lampe ist dort. Sie ist neu.

grammar.title: Negation and compound nouns
grammar.explanation: Place nicht before the adjective or phrase being negated: Das Zimmer ist nicht teuer. Compound nouns are written together; the final noun determines the article.

grammar.title: The final noun gives a compound its article
grammar.explanation: German compound nouns are written as one word. The final noun determines the gender and article: der Tisch → der Schreibtisch; die Maschine → die Waschmaschine.

grammar.title: Comparing housing information
grammar.explanation: Use the unchanged adjective after sein to describe a room or an offer. Add nicht before the adjective to make a negative statement.

grammar.title: Clock time, weekdays and schedules
grammar.explanation: Use um for clock times, am for weekdays and parts of the day, and von ... bis ... for a time span. German halb acht means 7:30.
examples: Am Montag arbeite ich von neun bis fünf.

grammar.title: Opening times and verb position
grammar.explanation: In a main clause, the conjugated verb stays in position two even if a time phrase comes first. Read opening notices for opens, closes and closed days.

Von acht bis zwölf Uhr lernt sie.

grammar.title: Separable and non-separable verbs
grammar.explanation: In aufstehen and anrufen, the stressed prefix separates and goes to the end in a main clause. In arbeiten, there is no separable prefix.
examples: Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf.

grammar.title: Time phrase first, verb still second
grammar.explanation: A time phrase can come first for emphasis, but the conjugated verb remains in position two. The subject then comes after the verb.
examples: Am Morgen stehe ich früh auf.
Um neun Uhr fängt der Kurs an.

grammar.title: Present-tense stem changes in common routine verbs
grammar.explanation: Some common verbs change their vowel with du or er/sie: essen → du isst; schlafen → er schläft; fernsehen → du siehst fern.

grammar.title: ja / nein / doch
grammar.explanation: doch is used to contradict a negative question
examples: Hast du keine Zeit? – Doch, ich habe Zeit.
Kommst du nicht? – Doch, ich komme.

grammar.title: Masculine accusative article change
grammar.explanation: A masculine direct object changes der to den and ein to einen. Feminine and neuter articles do not change in these examples.

grammar.title: Changing verbs: nehmen, lesen, treffen, fahren
grammar.explanation: Several common verbs change their stem vowel in the singular: du nimmst / er nimmt, du liest / er liest, du triffst / er trifft, du fährst / er fährt.
examples: Hast du keine Zeit? – Doch, am Abend.

grammar.title: Accusative for the thing you do or choose
grammar.explanation: With many verbs, the direct object answers “what?”. A masculine noun changes der → den and ein → einen; feminine die/eine and neuter das/ein stay the same.

grammar.title: Answering a negative question
grammar.explanation: Use doch when you want to contradict a negative question. Use nein when you agree that the negative statement is true; ja confirms a positive statement.
examples: Hast du keinen Hunger? – Doch, ich habe Hunger.
Hast du keine Zeit? – Nein, heute nicht.

grammar.title: Sentence stress in a yes/no exchange
grammar.explanation: In spoken answers, the important information word receives the strongest stress. Practise keeping the German question melody while making the contrast clear.
examples: Fährst du am Samstag? – Ja, am Samstag.
Regnet es? – Nein, die Sonne scheint.

grammar.title: Modal verbs können & wollen
grammar.explanation: Modal verb in position 2, main verb at the end in infinitive

grammar.title: Perfekt with haben
grammar.explanation: Most verbs use haben + past participle

grammar.title: Perfekt with sein
grammar.explanation: Verbs of movement and change of state use sein

grammar.title: Word order with modal verbs
grammar.explanation: Conjugate können or wollen in position two. Put the second verb in the infinitive at the end of the main clause.
examples: Die Kinder wollen im Park spielen.

grammar.title: Perfect tense: auxiliary and participle position
grammar.explanation: In a main clause, the conjugated auxiliary haben or sein is in position two and the participle is at the end. Many movement verbs use sein; most other verbs use haben.

grammar.title: Making and responding to plans
grammar.explanation: Ask about availability, suggest a time, accept with Ja, gern or decline politely with Leider kann ich nicht. Give another possible time when you can.
examples: Ja, gern. Wann treffen wir uns?
Leider kann ich am Vormittag nicht.

grammar.title: Perfekt: the auxiliary is second, participle is last
grammar.explanation: In a normal past-tense statement, haben or sein is conjugated in position two; the past participle goes at the end. Keep nicht before the participle when negating the action.
examples: Wir sind am Samstag nach Hause gefahren.

grammar.title: Build common participles
grammar.explanation: Many regular verbs use ge- + stem + -t; some common forms are irregular and should be learned as a pair. Movement or change-of-place verbs often use sein.

grammar.title: Polite suggestions and alternatives
grammar.explanation: Use Hast du Lust ...? or Wollen wir ...? to suggest an activity. Accept with gern; decline politely with leider and, if possible, suggest another time.
examples: Hast du Lust, ins Kino zu gehen?
Leider kann ich heute nicht. Geht es morgen?

exercises.exampleAnswer: Gestern habe ich Deutsch gelernt. Mein Sohn ist heute krank und kann nicht zur Schule kommen.
exercises.pronunciationBn: গেস্টার্ন হাবে ইখ ডয়চ গেলেয়ার্ন্ট। মাইন জোন ইস্ট হয়টে ক্রাঙ্ক উন্ট কান নিখ্ট ৎসুয়া শুলে কোমেন।

exercises.question: Choose the correct sentence.
Complete: Gestern _____ ich zu Hause geblieben.
Many movement verbs form Perfekt with sein.
Which is a polite explanation for missing school?
Complete: Bitte seien Sie _____. (on time)
After können, a second verb stays in the infinitive at the end.
Parent letter: The class trip is Friday. Children need a packed lunch and must arrive by 08:15. What should a child bring?
exercises.explanation: The parent letter lists what children need for the trip.

exercises.question: Complete: Gestern _____ ich meine Hausaufgaben gemacht.
exercises.explanation: machen forms Perfekt with haben.

exercises.question: Which sentence reports a movement in the past correctly?
exercises.explanation: gehen forms the Perfekt with sein and the participle gegangen.

exercises.question: Tell a friend three things you did yesterday. Use one haben verb and one movement verb with sein.
exercises.exampleAnswer: Gestern habe ich Deutsch gelernt. Danach habe ich mit meiner Schwester gekocht. Am Abend bin ich nach Hause gegangen.
exercises.explanation: Put the participle at the end and select the correct auxiliary.
exercises.pronunciationBn: গেস্টার্ন হাবে ইখ ডয়চ গেলেয়ার্ন্ট। ডানাখ হাবে ইখ মিট মাইনার শ্ভেস্টার গেকোখ্ট। আম আবেন্ট বিন ইখ নাখ হাউসে গেগাঙ্গেন।

exercises.question: Write a short absence note to a teacher. Include the child's name, date and a simple reason.
exercises.exampleAnswer: Guten Morgen, mein Sohn Amir kann heute, am 12. Mai, nicht in die Schule kommen. Er ist krank und hat Fieber. Freundliche Grüße, Amina Das.
exercises.explanation: Include a greeting, name, date, reason and closing.

exercises.question: The sentence “Ich bin meine Hausaufgaben gemacht” is correct.
exercises.explanation: machen uses haben: Ich habe meine Hausaufgaben gemacht.

exercises.question: Match each infinitive with its participle.
exercises.explanation: Learn frequent infinitive-participle pairs.

exercises.question: Complete the modal sentence: Wir _____ morgen die Lehrerin anrufen. (can)
exercises.explanation: With a modal verb, the second verb stays infinitive at the end.
exercises.pronunciationBn: ভিয়া ক্যোনেন মর্গেন ডি লেয়ারারিন আনরুফেন।

exercises.question: Put a school absence call in order.
items: Mein Sohn kann heute nicht kommen.
Guten Morgen. Hier ist Amina Das.
exercises.explanation: Identify yourself, explain the absence, then respond to the school.

exercises.question: A school note says “Bitte melden Sie Amir bis 08:00 krank.” What should the parent do?
options: Call or notify the school before 08:00.
Bring Amir to the library at 08:00.
exercises.explanation: krankmelden means report an illness.

exercises.question: Write a short reply accepting a class outing invitation. Include the day and meeting time.
exercises.exampleAnswer: Hallo Rafi, ja, ich komme gern mit. Am Samstag um 10 Uhr bin ich am Bahnhof. Viele Grüße, Amir.
exercises.explanation: State clearly that you accept and repeat the time/place.

exercises.question: Which word has the spelling sch?
exercises.explanation: Schule begins with sch; practise the three-letter sound together.

exercises.question: Practise sch, st and sp at the start of words: Schule, Stunde, Sport, spielen. Then use two in a sentence.
exercises.exampleAnswer: Am Samstag spiele ich Sport in der Schule.
exercises.explanation: Say the consonant cluster clearly, then speak the sentence naturally.
exercises.pronunciationBn: আম জামস্টাক শ্পিলে শ্পোর্ট ইন ডেয়া শুলে।

exercises.question: Complete a polite decline: Leider _____ ich heute nicht kommen.
exercises.explanation: Use kann ich nicht to give a polite reason.

exercises.question: After wollen, the second verb normally stays in the infinitive at the end.
exercises.explanation: For example: Wir wollen am Samstag fahren.

exercises.question: Which is a polite alternative after declining a plan?
options: Leider kann ich heute nicht. Geht es morgen?
exercises.explanation: A polite decline can offer another time.

exercises.question: Write a short message to the school about an absence. Use krank, heute and one past-tense sentence about yesterday's homework.
exercises.exampleAnswer: Guten Morgen, mein Sohn Amir ist heute krank und kann nicht in die Schule kommen. Gestern hat er seine Hausaufgaben gemacht. Freundliche Grüße, Amina.
exercises.explanation: Check the present absence, a clear Perfekt sentence, greeting and closing.

exercises.question: Suggest an outing, accept or decline, and give a new time if needed.
exercises.exampleAnswer: Hast du Lust, am Sonntag zum See zu fahren? – Leider kann ich Sonntag nicht. Geht es am Samstag? – Ja, gern.
exercises.explanation: Practise the full exchange, not just the invitation.
exercises.pronunciationBn: হাস্ট ডু লুস্ট, আম জোনটাক ৎসুম জে ৎসু ফারেন? – লাইডার কান ইখ জোনটাক নিখ্ট। গেট এস আম জামস্টাক? – ইয়া, গেয়ান।

exercises.question: Complete the spelling pattern: _____ule (school).
exercises.explanation: Schule begins with sch; keep the three letters together.
exercises.pronunciationBn: শুলে

exercises.question: Which word begins with st?
exercises.explanation: Stunde begins with st; Schule begins with sch and Sprache with sp.

exercises.question: Short exam-style note: Write two or three sentences to your teacher explaining why you cannot come today and when you hope to return.
exercises.exampleAnswer: Guten Morgen, ich bin heute krank und kann nicht zum Deutschkurs kommen. Ich hoffe, dass ich morgen wieder da bin. Viele Grüße, Amina
exercises.explanation: Include a greeting, reason, today/return information and a closing.
